newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir prepares for rendezvous with relief crew.
newsitem.headline: Mir prepares for rendezvous with relief crew.

text.p: The crew aboard the ailing space station Mir was preparing on Thursday to welcome aboard two new cosmonauts who will later undertake repairs vital to the future of the orbiting craft, officials said.

"The docking will take place at 21:03 (1703 GMT) and then they'll open the hatch at about 22:30 (1830 GMT)," said Mission Control spokesman Valery Lyndin. "They'll meet in the base block and there will be, we can say, a holiday spirit."

The arriving commander Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, 43, will also bring fresh food and souvenirs from Earth, which will add to the festive mood for the current Russian crew, in orbit since February.
The two crews will share the quarters on Mir, a collection of different modules, until August 14, when current commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin return to Earth.
British-American physicist Michael Foale will remain on board until late September when NASA astronaut David Wolf, who is now in training outside Moscow, is scheduled to replace him.

The festive atmosphere of welcoming the new crew is unlikely to last for long. Mir has been running on partial power since June 25 when it collided with its resupply ship and since last week the Elektron oxygen generating system has not worked.
A back-up oxygen system is also off because the entire Kvant-2 module housing it was shut down to conserve energy after the June collision.
The crew was relying on its two-month supply of oxygen candles, officials said.
The Mir crew continued to work on the Elektron on Thursday, but was focused mostly on the later docking with the Soyuz capsule carrying Solovyov and Vinogradov.
"They have to prepare the ship, check that the systems are in order and work according to set instructions," Lyndin said.

The spokesman said arriving cosmonaut Vinogradov, a newcomer to space, was in fine condition on Thursday after being "overcome with emotions" during take-off, according to Mission Control's chief doctor.
"Of course (Vinogradov) was worried, and perhaps he was to a certain extent overcome by emotions," Igor Goncharov, deputy flight director overseeing medical issues, told Reuters on Wednesday.

Goncharov said equipment measuring the cosmonauts' heart and pulse rates during the Tuesday launch registered a considerably calmer disposition from Solovyov, one of Russia's most experienced cosmonauts, who has flown four times on Mir for a total of 456 days in space.

Vinogradov will lead risky efforts to restore power on Mir by opening the hatch to the airless, darkened Spektr module on August 20 and reconnecting cables that lead to solar panels outside. Success in the operation will restore much of Mir's energy supply.
